issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette: Ahmed, a 75-year-old widowed sculptor with Middle Eastern heritage, has been grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred several months ago. The incident involved a serious fall from his studio loft, resulting in multiple fractures and a prolonged recovery period. Since then, Ahmed’s world has become a landscape of constant vigilance and self-doubt. The traumatic event has left Ahmed deeply entrenched in thoughts about why such an ordeal befell him. He constantly seeks meaning in the accident, pondering whether there was something he could have done differently to prevent it. This relentless search for answers stems from his belief that his body is no longer reliable. "I can no longer trust my own body," he often says with a sense of resignation. The fractures and subsequent surgeries have left him feeling permanently damaged, both physically and emotionally. Ahmed’s fear of physical vulnerability has led to significant changes in how he interacts with the world around him. He now avoids any situations that put his body under stress, such as climbing ladders or lifting heavy materials necessary for his sculpting work. His studio, once a vibrant space filled with creative energy, is now a place of cautious movements and constant self-monitoring. Ahmed frequently checks his body for signs of danger or injury, often pausing mid-stroke to assess whether he feels any discomfort. The weight of these negative appraisals has profoundly influenced the way Ahmed copes. His belief that he has permanently changed for the worse drives him to engage in maladaptive strategies like meaning-seeking and body monitoring. He spends hours ruminating on why the accident happened, often feeling a sense of helplessness and despair. "I have permanently changed for the worse," he says with deep sorrow, as if the fall has cast an indelible shadow over his life. This constant search for answers has also led Ahmed to avoid physical stress at all costs. He no longer goes up onto the loft where he used to create some of his most intricate pieces. This avoidance has taken a toll on his work and his sense of identity as a sculptor. "I can’t even pick up a chisel without worrying if I’ll hurt myself," he laments. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was the realization that these behaviors were isolating him from the life he once cherished. He is most afraid of losing his ability to create and connect with others through his art. Despite his fears, he hopes to regain a sense of trust in his body and find ways to continue pursuing his passion for sculpture without being held back by the constant fear of physical vulnerability. Ahmed’s story is one of resilience in the face of profound adversity. His struggle to reconcile his past trauma with his present reality has led him to seek support, hoping that through therapy he can navigate these challenges and reconnect with the vibrant creative spirit that once defined him.
